widgets.title: Introduction
widgets.text:
We all love playing Connections - it's a succinct, bite-sized puzzle which accompanies your morning coffee. It's a great formula, but experienced players don't get to sink their teeth into it; Let's give them something with a bit more substance - something that will transfix them for the entire day.

I've designed this puzzle format because Connections is my favorite NYT game and I'd love to see a long-form version of it. This take on the Connections formula involves a layout where categories intersect, allowing single phrases to have multiple interpretations depending on the categories they're apart of. The closest comparison I can think of is how Wordle would be logically adapted into a Scrabble-like format. But, this dichotomy already exists on your roster - the Crossword and the Mini deliver the same gameplay premise simultaneously in both long and short formats.

widgets.title: Cross Connections
widgets.text: Click to play. Best on desktop, in fullscreen. ESC to close.

widgets.title: How to play
widgets.text:
Each phrase (right) belongs in a cell on the layout (left). the layout is arranged such that every line of four cells contains four phrases which have something in common with each other, forming a category. these categories intersect, making junction points. A phrase which belongs on a junction point will have two different interpretations simultaneously, pertaining to their respective categories. 

Some phrases have already been placed in for you; They garner colors which represent their category's difficulty. Yellow categories are easy- they are four words that can be taken at face value, such as synonyms or themed pop culture references. Then goes green, then blue, and finally purple. Purple categories are very tricky, sneaky, and obscure, and are often not very related to the phrases themselves; but rest assured all categories will always follow a single, consistent, unifying rule.

widgets.title: Nuances
widgets.text:
- One phrase in each category is already revealed, including it's difficulty. Not only does this 'anchor' the puzzle and prevent players from inputting categories wherever they want, but revealing the color allows them to break down the puzzle and work through it in a semi-linear fashion, as opposed to being completely left in the dark (this system is what you already do in standard connections games, you just call it a 'hint', accessible on a different page).

- It's good to start with the yellows, as they can be taken at face value and will be the easiest to figure out; it helps to establish the board and remove fluff from the phrase list. However, it's possible a category of any difficulty could be immediately apparent to the player (in which case there's no downside to establishing it early on).

- The junction points are also very powerful, as you'd need to look though the phrase list to find what applies to both categories. No 'junction word' will ever have the same meaning in both categories, so referencing the given phrases in relation to their junction point could help you find out the hidden multiple interpretations of any phrase.

- The loops are what really brings the puzzle together - when players are struggling with a category, they can tackle it from an alternative method by solving the intersecting categories, in order to loop back around and solve a different junction point in the initial category. If done effectively, it helps greatly in two ways: 3/4 of phrases in the single category are revealed AND a lot of phrases get removed from the word bank, narrowing down the possible solutions. 

- I also hypothesized an opt-in 'Hard Mode' which would add an interesting twist - every puzzle now includes one additional phrase in it's list, which does NOT belong to any cell. Given the puzzlemaker can choose whatever phrase they want, it not only gives opportunity for true red herrings, but also removes the standard 'process of elimination' mentality that a near-complete puzzle usually fosters.  

- The format here is also extremely malleable; these puzzles feature 10 categories with 4 phrases each, but we can easily raise/lower those values as we please. Maybe every puzzle should be centered around one 'theme' category with 5-8 phrases in it? Maybe we scale the size of puzzles to 12-16 categories - these numbers could be anything. However, through limited testing, I've found 10-12 is the sweet spot; going higher results in too many words in the phrase box and the puzzle gets exponentially harder to comb through and digest for the player.

widgets.title: Why Bother?
widgets.text:
It's no doubt NYT's Games branch has become an incredibly valuable pillar of NYT as a whole. Frequent experimentation with concepts like Vertex, Zorse, Capture, and Digits tell me you're open to new ideas.

Players deserve a new challenge once they've mastered Connections - and the metrics tell us plenty of players are ready for something new.

widgets.title: Origin
widgets.text: Exul Omnium started as a simple desire to make an original trading card game. I discovered a website called Artbreeder in 2020 which hosted some of the earliest stable diffusion models. It couldn't recieve prompts, and instead had hardcoded 'types' of images that could be formed. There were four types: full body figures, landscapes, abstract 'album art', and headshots. Of those options, I found the first two the most workable and formed my game concept with only two types of cards.

widgets.title: Early Mechanics
widgets.text:
The core design philosophy in my approach was simple: no gameplay-necessary text. Every card's ability would be detailed by an arrangement of symbols and icons. Eight "Factions" were created, where "Entity" cards need to be matched by type with "Land" cards in order for the Entity's abilities to work. 

One highly-experimental decision of mine which I was quite worred about in practice was homogenizing Health and Damage into a single Strength value. What this means is an Entity that has 10 "Health" also deals 10 "Damage"; if it takes 9 Damage, it is now one point away from death and is only capable of dealing 1 "Damage". I imagine this as the Entity's fortitude - a heavily damaged and wounded creature won't be capable of producing attacks with the same proficiency as if it were fully healthy. To complement this system, both attackers deal their damage at the same time. Two entities with 10 Strength will completely defeat each other simultaneously, thus it's wise to pick weaker opponents. 

When you see D followed by a number, it refers to a size of dice. On deploying an Entity, you roll the specified dice for it's Strength value. It also has a concrete value that gets added to, for some degree of certainty. This allows cards to fall into a "range" of possible Strength values when they enter the battlefield. After that, the Strength value will only change when the Entity recieves damage. 

Split Faction Lands allow Entities of different types to share the same land. However, Split Faction Entities are less of a benefit - they require more specific Land types for their ability to work. Lands have a limited capacity that is permanently lost when an Entity within it dies. Lands also had their own abilities they can impart on their inhabitants.

widgets.title: Reflection
widgets.text:
Physical cards were soon printed, and a handful of playtests begun. While the game worked, the ability formatting proved to be too obscure for smooth gameplay. There overall wasn't enough substance to make gameplay interesting; weirdly enough, I was limited by what I could make the ACSII symbols represent - it got heiroglyphic very quickly and I chose simplicity at the cost of less interesting ability variations.

My personal interest in the project waned down, and was quickly forgotten as I shifted focus to better things.

widgets.title: Second Approach
widgets.text: in 2022, I discovered Midjourney - a prompt-based image generator with significantly more freedom. The Exul Omnium flame has been reignited, and I returned with more tricks up my sleeve. Firstly, I became very adept with Blender and used it's vector-based features to form my card layouts. Secondly, I found a proper card manufacturer - no more hand-cutting printer paper cardstock with household scissors.

widgets.title: Polished Mechanics
widgets.text:
The ability system needed the biggest revamp. The system from The Battle Cats was very attractive to me - units can have 'traits' which act like passive strengths during combat. The units could also have specific types it exclusively targets. I worked off this principle to form Abilities, which contain both the trigger and the effect. The target type is determined by the coloring behind the Ability's icon.

The rest of the game's philosophies stayed relatively unchanged; eight Factions, two card types, identical Strength system. The full body artwork was no longer necessary - it's a remnant of Artbreeder's system which I decided to maintain into Midjourney. I felt a full body depiction framed the Entity more clinically, like a prison's booking photo. Thus, the "Attacker" cards got renamed to "Mercs" (Mercenaries).

Heaps of abilities were soon arranged, and I had to quickly set up a wiki guide website for all of them.

widgets.title: Finalization
widgets.text:
With over 100 cards made with the new format, playtests started up again. The new format was much more fun and understandable. A microculture arose where players would let their opponent make important chance rolls for maximum fairness. The only caveat with this system was that it became difficult to track all the relevant perk abilities in play throughout combat. This issue pointed to the reality that this system would be more conducive digitally, where a computer could keep track of all the abilities for you; but that would raise it's own concerns regarding the magnitude of chance-based mechanics and the reality of randomly-generated values. Side note: Split lands provide a consistent 2 Merc slots, but variants exist where they player rolls an initial D4 for the land capacity. Statistically, a 1-4 chance is better than a flat 2 -- but the 25% instances where the player would roll 1, they found the rare occurance so debilitating to their game they actually PREFERRED the concrete certaintly of a flat 2. This reinforced to me how much players value certainty in a game built around RNG, even when rolling the dice offered better returns. 

As the card count grew, I started reaching out to real artists -- a mixture of commissions and directly buying their premade artwork. These cards were significantly more appealing than the generated ones but, between cost and speed, generating the images was much, much quicker. So I did both.

Now, with over 300 cards, I looked to replicate some more facets of popular TCGs: Holographic cards. My manufacturers were capable of producing this, and the look was too enticing to pass up. I created a secondary graphical look which I never properly named--Glass or Elite--which involved a transparent glass-like border which looked very sleek and showed off more of the artwork behind it. Previously white elements were recolored gold. Assuredly a gem in any deck.

widgets.title: So where is Exul Omnium now?
widgets.text:
As the public opinions of AI-generated art developed sour, I foresaw incredibly poor reception with the project as a whole; my original outlook was that the imagery wasn't necssary at all--not for any TCG for that matter--and had no bearing on actual gameplay. Imagery brings in a lot of visual appeal, and with Exul Omnium's graphical style showing off even more of the artwork than usual, to say it would be a bad look is an understatement.

I understand the grievances and, while the entire project is essentially ready for deployment, the game is stuck in a limbo until every single card could be replaced with human-made artwork (which is not a high personal priority of mine). So it sits, collecting dust, waiting...
